warmup.q: A store keeps 3 copies of each payment. A write counts as done once 2 copies have it, and a read asks all 3 and returns the newer of the first 2 answers. A write that marks a payment captured (its money has moved) is still on its way. The fraud checker's read returns captured. 5 ms after that read ends, the ledger starts a read. What can it return?
options: Only captured: any 2 copies share at least one copy with any other 2
captured or the old status: the write may be on one copy so far, and the ledger's first two answers can both come from copies without it
An error, because a write is still in progress
Always the old status, because the write hasn't finished yet
warmup.why: The overlap between any two groups of 2 only helps with writes that have finished. This one is still on its way, so it may sit on one copy so far, which the fraud checker's read happened to reach. The ledger asks all three and takes the first two answers. If those come from the two copies the write hasn't reached yet, it returns the old status. A read that starts after another read saw the new value, and returns the old one, breaks linearizable. The first option is the tempting one. The fix, where the reader copies the value to a second copy before answering, is in the fourth section.

sections.h: One copy, one instant: what linearizable demands
sections.html:
Let's turn the café owner's problem into four programs and one value. The payments app keeps each payment's status as a number. 1 means authorized: the money is set aside on the card. 2 means captured: it has moved to the shop. The capture program writes status = 2 for one payment, and the write takes 60 ms from request to answer. Meanwhile, three other programs read the status: the ledger, which keeps the account books, the fraud checker, which looks for suspicious payments, and the email program, which sends receipts.

A value you can read and write, like this status, is called a register. As in Consistency models, each operation is a bar on a timeline, from when the request is sent to when the answer comes back. The stepper below draws the four bars.

In 1990, Maurice Herlihy and Jeannette Wing gave the exact rule. A history is linearizable if every operation seems to take effect at one instant somewhere inside its bar. Taken in the order of those instants, the operations must give the answers one plain copy would give. That instant is the operation's linearization point. It's a thought experiment: the store never reports it. We ask whether any choice of points works.

Step through the stepper, and three things fall out.

A read that overlaps a write may return the old value or the new one. While the capture is on its way, the ledger saw the old status and the fraud checker saw the new one, and both are fine.

Once any read has returned the new value, every read that starts later must return it too, or something newer. This is the rule that catches systems with copies, because "send the write to every copy, sooner or later" doesn't enforce it. The email program's read started after the fraud checker's had already seen 2, so it must see 2.

The order that matters is real time. The fraud checker and the email program run on different computers. If they never talk, how could anyone notice the stale read? Through any second channel. The fraud checker announces "captured", and the email program reacts and reads the old status. That's the café owner's message and her empty list, and the third section comes back to it.

Herlihy and Wing proved one more thing the lab relies on: linearizability is local. A history is linearizable exactly when, for each value, the operations on that value are. So a checker can take each key, the name a value is stored under, on its own. Sequential consistency doesn't work this way. The lab of Consistency models has a test with two keys, where each key on its own is sequential and the whole history isn't.

In the definition, the word "seems" carries the weight. Inside, a store may do anything: hold writes back, copy them, retry them. What it may not do is let any client see something that one copy, changing at one instant per operation, couldn't have produced. Next, we'll turn the stepper's search by hand into a program.

try.title: Check the stepper's history
steps: Open CheckerDemo.kt. It writes the stepper's history with the lab's builder and checks it. Then it checks it again with the email program's read changed to return 2.
Predict the search steps: will the bad history take more steps than the good one, or fewer?
try.expect:
as recorded: linearizable no (7 search steps)
  longest prefix: ledger:r(status)=-@5-15, capture:w(status,2)@0-60, fraud:r(status)=2@20-30
with email's read returning 2: linearizable yes (6 search steps)
  linearization: ledger:r(status)=-@5-15, capture:w(status,2)@0-60, fraud:r(status)=2@20-30, email:r(status)=2@40-50

The failing check reports the longest prefix it could build, the longest start of an order that works: ledger, then the write, then fraud. Email's read can't be added after that, and no other start gets further. That prefix is where you begin reading when a real checker rejects a history. Both histories are tiny, so both checks take a handful of steps.

sections.h: Checking a history: a search for the order
sections.html:
Placing points by hand works for four bars. A real test records thousands, so we want a program that does it, a checker. It takes a history and a description of how one plain copy behaves. For a register, a read returns the current value and a write replaces it. A compare-and-set writes a new value only if the current one equals an expected value. Then the checker searches for a linearization. Jeannette Wing and Chun Gong described the classic search in 1993, and every tool since builds on it.

The search builds the order one operation at a time. At each step, it may take any operation that is minimal: not yet placed, and no other unplaced operation finished before it started. Putting a minimal operation next can't break real-time order. The checker asks whether that operation's recorded answer is possible from the current value. If it is, the checker places it and goes on. If that path dead-ends, it takes the operation back and tries the next one. If every path dead-ends, the history isn't linearizable. The worked example below runs this by hand.

Gavin Lowe added the improvement that makes it practical. Two different paths often reach the same situation: the same operations placed, and the same value in the register. Remember every situation you've explored, and never explore one twice. With that memory, called a cache, the lab's checker is about 40 lines.

Even so, checking is hard in general. Gibbons and Korach proved in 1997 that it's NP-complete, which means no known method is fast on every history. The cost grows with concurrency, the number of operations whose bars overlap, since each overlap is a choice of order. The length of the history matters much less. The Try-it shows the growth: with 8 clients overlapping, a history the checker must reject takes thousands of steps with the cache, and more than five million without it.

You may meet three tools. Knossos is the checker from Jepsen, the company that tests databases. It runs two searches side by side and takes whichever finishes first, and it still struggles past a few hundred heavily overlapping operations. Porcupine, written in the Go language, is a Wing and Gong search with Lowe's cache that also splits the history by key, thanks to locality. Its project page reports it as 1,000 to 10,000 times faster than Knossos on Jepsen's histories. etcd, a small database that many programs use to share settings, tests itself with it. Lincheck, from JetBrains (version 3.7), checks classes in Java and Kotlin. A thread is one line of work inside a program. You mark a class's methods with @Operation, and Lincheck calls them from several threads at once, or steps through the possible orders itself. Then it checks the results for linearizability. It's the tool to reach for when you write a class that many threads share.

Next, we'll ask which jobs need this promise at all.

try.title: Watch the search cost grow with concurrency
steps: Run CheckerDemo with -Pargs=cost. It builds histories from one plain copy, with 2 to 8 clients overlapping. It makes the last read return a value nobody wrote, so the checker must try everything before it says no. It counts search steps with and without Lowe's cache, and gives up at 5,000,000.
Before you run it, guess the step count for 8 clients with the cache.
try.expect:
clients  ops   steps with cache   steps without cache
      2   12                 31                   342
      3   18                120                 25454
      4   24                341           > 5,000,000
      5   30               1137           > 5,000,000
      6   36               2645           > 5,000,000
      7   42               6896           > 5,000,000
      8   48              17117           > 5,000,000

Without the cache, 3 clients already take 25,454 steps, and 4 clients more than five million. With it, the count still grows two and a half to four times with each extra client: 17,117 steps for 48 operations. Real checkers add more tricks, such as splitting by key and smarter ordering, but none removes the growth. That's why Jepsen keeps the overlap low when it checks for linearizable.

sections.h: Which jobs need it: one winner, one owner, one story across channels
sections.html:
Most data doesn't need linearizable. A shop's screen of today's sales can be a second behind. Three kinds of job do need it, and a payments app has all three.

The first is choosing a leader, or handing out a lock: a token that lets one program at a time do something, such as run the nightly payout to shops. A lock service must give it to at most one holder. If the store behind the service can return stale reads, two programs can both read "free", both write "mine", and both believe they won. That's called split brain. The lesson Leases, locks and fencing tokens depended on exactly this. It added fencing tokens, numbers that grow with each new holder, because even a correct lock can't stop a holder that paused and woke up late. That counter must never go backwards, and that needs linearizable too. ZooKeeper and etcd, small databases built for this, exist mostly to provide these tools, and lesson 5 covers them.

The second is a rule of the "only one" or "never below zero" kind. A request number, which lets the app spot a payment sent twice, may be claimed by one request. A card number may belong to one account. Seat 12A may be sold once. A balance may never go negative. Each needs every copy to agree on one up-to-date value at the moment of the decision: a linearizable compare-and-set, or a single leader that does the check. Some rules can be loosened on purpose. An airline sells more seats than it has and pays the passengers it bumps. A card company approves a small payment when the bank can't be reached and settles up later. That's a business decision, made knowingly.

The third is timing across channels, the café owner's problem. The checkout saves a payment to the database, then announces "payment saved" on a second channel. Many apps use Kafka for this, a program that passes messages between other programs. The program that pays shops picks up the message and reads the payment from a follower. (The database keeps copies on several computers. One, the leader, takes every write first and passes it on to the others, the followers.) The message arrived in 5 ms, and the follower is 40 ms behind. The program finds no payment, marks the message as failed and moves on. Nothing was lost, yet the two channels disagree, and the payout is wrong. The message carried timing ("this happened"), and the follower didn't respect it.

There are three fixes. Read from the leader for anything a message triggers. Or put a position in the message: the leader's place in its list of changes, as in the lesson When followers lag. The follower waits until it has reached that place. Or put the data in the message itself, so there's nothing to look up.

All three jobs share something: a decision that must not be made twice, or a fact that one party has seen and another must not miss. If neither applies, a weaker model is cheaper and fine. A read that decides something must see every finished write. Send it to the leader. Next, we'll see which ways of keeping copies can give it.

refs.title: Kleppmann, How to do distributed locking

sections.h: Which ways of keeping copies give it, and why majorities alone don't
sections.html:
Go through the ways of keeping copies from the Replication track, and ask of each: can a client ever see something one copy couldn't produce?

One leader: it can be linearizable, if every read and write goes to the leader and the leader really is the leader. Both conditions fail in practice. Reading from followers is the usual way to spread the load, and the Try-it measures what that costs: 424 of 1,000 simulated histories weren't linearizable. A leader cut off by a partition, a break in the network, may also keep answering reads while a new leader takes writes elsewhere. And a failover, where another copy takes over from a failed leader, can lose writes the old leader had confirmed, as the lesson One leader, many followers showed. A write that finished is gone, which breaks it too.

Consensus, a way for several computers to agree on one decision (Paxos, Raft and Zab, in lessons 3 to 5), makes the leader question safe. A majority must agree on who leads, and on every write. Writes are then linearizable. Reads are linearizable only if the leader checks that it's still the leader before it answers. That's why etcd's linearizable read costs a round trip, a message there and an answer back, to a majority. Lesson 4, on Raft, covers the two ways to do that check.

Many leaders: no. Two leaders accept conflicting writes at the same time, by design.

No leader, with quorums: no, and this surprises people. A quorum is how many copies must answer. With 3 copies, a write might wait for w = 2 and a read for r = 2. The lesson Leaderless replication showed that when w + r is more than n, the number of copies, every group of readers overlaps every group of writers. The figure shows the race. A write of 9 reaches R1 quickly, and R2 and R3 late. Reader A asks all three, hears first from R1 and R2, and returns the newer value, 9. Reader B starts after A has finished, hears first from R2 and R3, and returns 8. B started after A finished and saw an older value: not linearizable. The overlap promise is about finished writes. This one hadn't finished, and A's read showed it early.

The fix is for the reader to finish the job the writer started. Before returning 9, reader A writes 9 back to two copies and waits for them to confirm. Now any read that starts after A returns must meet a copy that holds 9. Writers read first, to pick a version number higher than any they see. This is the ABD algorithm, named after Hagit Attiya, Amotz Bar-Noy and Danny Dolev, and it makes reads and writes linearizable with no leader. It costs a second round trip on every read: 30.7 ms instead of 15.3 ms in the Try-it. And it can't give you compare-and-set: two writers can each pick "version 8" for different values. For that you need consensus, the next lesson's subject.

Real stores sit in between. Cassandra, a database with no leader, does wait for that write-back on a QUORUM read. But it orders writes by timestamps from the clocks of clients or servers, so clocks that drift break linearizable anyway. Its linearizable path is a separate one, the lightweight transaction, which runs Paxos. Riak, another database with no leader, doesn't wait for the write-back at all. Next, we'll count what linearizable costs.

try.title: Count the histories that break linearizable
steps: Run QuorumDemo. It records 1,000 histories from each of four stores (3 clients, 10 operations each, one key) on a simulated network where 10% of messages take up to 100 ms. Then it checks each history with the lab's checker.

Predict the four counts first. Then read the bottom of the output: the first bad quorum history, around the read the checker couldn't place. c1 to c3 are the clients, and each line is one operation with its start and end in ms.
try.expect:
store                                     bad histories   mean read ms
single leader, reads at the leader              0 of 1000           21.0
single leader, reads at the follower          424 of 1000           21.2
quorum n=3 w=2 r=2                             20 of 1000           15.3
quorum n=3 w=2 r=2, sync read repair            0 of 1000           30.7

seed 5, the operations around c2's read at 218 ms (the checker's first unplaceable op):
    76-99   c3  w(balance,7)     ============
   121-195  c3  r(balance)=7                           ======================================
   136-163  c1  w(balance,8)                                   ==============
   165-230  c1  w(balance,9)                                                 =================================
   176-191  c2  r(balance)=9                                                       ========
   195-205  c2  r(balance)=9                                                                ======
   203-219  c3  r(balance)=9                                                                    =========
   211-218  c2  r(balance)=9                                                                        ====
   218-233  c2  r(balance)=8                                                                            ========
   223-245  c3  w(balance,10)                                                                             ============
   233-243  c1  r(balance)=9                                                                                   ======

Follower reads fail often. The plain quorum store fails rarely, 20 of 1,000, which is exactly why the bug survives testing. With the write-back, which the output calls synchronous read repair, none fail. In seed 5, w(balance,9) is on its way from 165 to 230 ms, and c2 reads 9 four times. Then c2's read at 218 ms reaches two copies that still hold 8 and returns it, older than what c2 itself saw a moment earlier. Note that the quorum reads are faster than the leader's (15.3 against 21.0 ms): a quorum read waits only for the fastest 2 of 3 replies.

sections.h: What it costs: waiting on every request, even inside your laptop
sections.html:
The first cost is time, paid with no failure anywhere. In 1994, Hagit Attiya and Jennifer Welch proved that a linearizable read or write must wait at least as long as the uncertainty in network delay. That's the gap between the fastest and the slowest a message might take. No cleverer method avoids it, while weaker models can answer from the copy at hand. etcd's own benchmark shows the size of it on one small cluster, a group of computers working together: three computers rented from Google Cloud, measured with etcd 3.2. One client doing linearizable reads got 1,353 reads a second, at 0.7 ms each. Reads that any member answers from its own copy, which etcd calls serializable (another meaning of the word), got 2,909 a second at 0.3 ms. With 1,000 clients, the numbers were 141,578 against 185,758 reads a second, at 5.5 ms against 2.2 ms. Across regions, the round trip is tens of milliseconds, and it lands on every read.

The second cost is availability, from the CAP section of Consistency models. A copy on the smaller side of a partition can't confirm it has the latest value, so it must refuse or wait.

The third cost sits in your laptop. Its processor (CPU) has several cores, each running its own thread. A multicore CPU isn't linearizable either, and it gives that up for speed, with no network in sight. Each core has a store buffer, a short queue where its writes wait before they reach the memory all cores share, so the core can carry on. Meanwhile, another core reads the old value. Java's JIT compiler, which turns your program into machine instructions while it runs, adds its own reordering: a write and a later read of a different variable may swap. The Try-it runs the classic test. Thread 1 writes x = 1, then reads y. Thread 2 writes y = 1, then reads x. In any single order of those four steps, at least one read comes after the other thread's write, so both reads returning 0 is impossible for one copy of memory. With plain arrays, it happened in hundreds of thousands of the five million trials, a different number on every run.

Java's answer is volatile, a word you put on a field that many threads share. The Java Memory Model, Java's rules for threads (section 17.4.4 of the language specification), puts every volatile read and write into one order that agrees with each thread's own order. Each volatile read sees the last write before it in that order. That's sequential consistency for those fields. HotSpot, the program that runs most Java code, pays for it with a fence, an instruction that makes the core finish its waiting memory operations before it goes on. On x86, the processor family in most PCs and servers, that's a locked instruction after each volatile write, which empties the store buffer. Java's ready-made classes for sharing data between threads, such as AtomicLong and ConcurrentHashMap, build on the same machinery.

So "one copy, one timeline" has the same price everywhere: someone waits until the others have caught up. On a CPU the wait is tens of nanoseconds (billionths of a second), in a data center about a millisecond, and across an ocean about 70 ms.

try.title: Catch your CPU reordering
steps: Run StoreBufferDemo. It runs 5,000,000 trials of the two-thread test above, first on plain IntArrays, then on AtomicIntegerArray, whose get and set behave like volatile fields. These are real threads on real cores, not a simulation.
Predict the plain count. Run it twice: does it change?
try.expect:
One run on an Apple M2 Max with JDK 25:

memory                             trials    both read 0
plain IntArray                  5,000,000      1,948,111
volatile (AtomicIntegerArray)    5,000,000              0

The plain count changes a lot from run to run (four runs here gave between about 670,000 and 1,950,000). It depends on the CPU, the JIT and whatever else is running, so expect your own numbers. The volatile count is always 0: the outcome is forbidden, and the fences make sure it never happens.

mistake: Reading from a follower when the read decides something. A program approves a refund by reading the payment from a follower, "to take load off the leader". It sees captured and refunds, while the leader already says refunded, because another request refunded it 30 ms earlier. Teams do this because follower reads are a standard tip for handling more traffic, and in tests the follower is never behind. The fix: send every read that decides something to the leader, or make the decision itself one conditional write on the leader ("refund only if still captured"). Keep follower reads for screens and reports, where a stale answer costs only a refresh.
opening:
A café owner's phone buzzes: "Payment received: 30.00." She opens the payments app to look at it, and the payment isn't in the list. She pulls down to refresh, and there it is.

The message and the list came from the same company and the same database. The message was sent after the payment was saved. The list read a copy that hadn't caught up yet.

It's easy to shrug at this. Each part did its job, and a second later everything agreed. But if the app had used that list to decide something, such as whether the payment could be refunded, a second is plenty of time to decide wrong.

In Consistency models, we put linearizable at the top of a ladder of promises: the copies behave like one. In this lesson, we'll pin down what that demands and check histories against it. Then we'll find the jobs that need it, the ways of keeping copies that give it, and the cost. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a café owner whose phone said a payment had arrived while her list said it hadn't. The message was a second channel, and the list read a copy that broke the rule of one copy, one timeline.

Look for the same thing in an app you use: a notification that opens a screen that doesn't show it yet. A parcel tracker, a shared document or a group chat will do. Each time, a second channel beat a copy.

Next, we'll find the tool that settles a race between two writers. It's a log of commands that every copy reads in the same order, with an agreement problem hiding underneath.

compare.title: A quorum read, without and with the write-back

a.label: plain quorum read
a.title: one round trip
a.html: override fun read(client: String, key: String, done: (Int?) -> Unit) = queryQuorum(key) { highest -> done(highest.value) // newest of r answers, even if only one replica has it }

b.label: ABD read
b.title: two round trips
b.html: override fun read(client: String, key: String, done: (Int?) -> Unit) = queryQuorum(key) { highest -> writeToQuorum(key, highest) { // make sure w replicas hold it done(highest.value) // only now may anyone see it } }

compare.note: The only difference is waiting for the value to reach two copies before answering. Without the wait, a read can show a write that's still on one copy, and a later read can miss it. With it, any read that starts afterwards meets a copy that holds the value. The price is a second round trip on every read, and it still gives no compare-and-set.

worked.title: Check a history by hand, the way the search does

steps.say: Write the history down as bars, sorted by start time. Here: a write of 9 from 0 to 50 ms, and three reads. The register held 8 before the write.
steps.code:
w(9)     0-50
r = 9   10-20
r = 8   30-40      <- 8 was the value before the write
r = 9   45-55

steps.say: Find the minimal operations: those that start no later than the earliest end among the operations not yet placed. At the start, the earliest end is 20 ms (the first read), so the write (starts at 0) and the first read (starts at 10) are minimal. The others start at 30 and 45, after 20.
steps.code:
unplaced ends: 50, 20, 40, 55  ->  min end 20
minimal: w(9) [starts 0], r=9 [starts 10]

steps.say: Try each minimal operation against the register, which holds 8 at the start. A read of 9 is impossible from 8. The write is possible: place it, and the value becomes 9.
steps.code: state 8: r=9? no      w(9)? yes -> state 9, placed {w}

steps.say: Go one level deeper. Now the first read (9) fits. Next, the only minimal operation is the read of 8 (the earliest end is now 40), and from the value 9 it's impossible. Back up: no other choice at any level leads anywhere, so the history isn't linearizable.
Name the cause in words. A read that began after another read had returned 9 returned 8, the older value: the register went back in time.
steps.code: r=9 (10-20) ended before r=8 (30-40) began, and r=8 is older: not linearizable

lab.title: A linearizability checker, run against two kinds of store
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder (no Docker, about a second). All 18 fail. Read History.kt: Op is one read, write or compare-and-set, with start and end times. Register.step(state, op) says whether an operation's recorded answer is possible from a state, and what the state becomes.

Exercise 1, Linearizability.checkKey: the Wing and Gong search. Sort the operations by start. Then, step by step: if every operation is placed, succeed. Otherwise find the earliest end among the unplaced ones, and try each unplaced operation that starts no later than that. Keep a HashSet of the (placed set, state) pairs you've already explored: that's Lowe's cache. Return the order on success and the longest prefix on failure, with a step count. check (given) runs it for each key.

CheckerTest and OraclePropertyTest check your search against hand-made histories, and against a slow search that tries every order, on 1,000 random ones. Then StoresTest records 200 histories from each store: the single leader passes, and follower reads and the plain quorum store fail.

Exercise 2, QuorumStore.finishRead: when syncReadRepair is true, write the value back with writeToQuorum, and answer only when that completes. The last two tests of StoresTest then pass: zero violations, and a read takes about twice as long.
hints: Use a java.util.BitSet for the placed set, and store placed.clone() as BitSet in the cache. If you store the live object, every entry changes when you change it.
Once the operations are sorted by start, you can break as soon as an unplaced one starts after the earliest end: every later one starts even later.
Track the longest prefix by copying path.toList() whenever the path gets longer than the best so far.
A bad seed replays exactly: record(seed) { QuorumStore(it) } gives the same history every time. So print it, and read it next to Linearizability.check(h).order.

drill.title: The search, from memory
drill.prompt: Write the core of a Wing and Gong search with Lowe's cache, for one register. Given operations sorted by start and Register.step(state, op), return whether a linearization exists. You may skip the step count and the longest prefix.

answer.html: fun linearizable(all: List<Op>): Boolean { val placed = BitSet(all.size) val seen = HashSet<Pair<BitSet, Int?>>() fun go(count: Int, state: Int?): Boolean { if (count == all.size) return true if (!seen.add((placed.clone() as BitSet) to state)) return false val minEnd = all.indices.filter { !placed[it] }.minOf { all[it].end } for (i in all.indices) { if (placed[i]) continue if (all[i].start > minEnd) break // not minimal, nor anything after it val (ok, next) = Register.step(state, all[i]) if (!ok) continue placed.set(i) if (go(count + 1, next)) return true placed.clear(i) // dead end: take it back } return false } return go(0, null) }

recap: Linearizable (Herlihy and Wing, 1990): each operation takes effect at one instant inside its bar, and those instants replay on one plain copy. Once any read sees a new value, every read that starts later must see it too.

Linearizability is local, so a checker can take each key on its own. Checking is NP-complete in general and grows with the number of overlapping operations. Wing and Gong's search with Lowe's cache is the basis of Knossos and Porcupine, and Lincheck does it for Java and Kotlin classes.
It's needed for leaders and locks, for "only one" and "never below zero" decisions, and wherever a second channel (a message, a phone call) tells someone that a write happened.

One leader gives it if every read goes to a leader that really is the leader, and consensus gives it if reads also check leadership. Many leaders and plain quorums don't. ABD (read, then write back to a quorum) fixes quorum reads and writes, at a second round trip.
It costs a round trip on every request (etcd measured 0.7 ms against 0.3 ms), refusals on the smaller side of a partition, and fences on a multicore CPU, which Java's volatile pays for you.

The limit: linearizable reads and writes still can't settle a race between two writers. ABD can't do compare-and-set, so two clients that both read "free" can both write "mine". Choosing between them takes consensus.

explain.prompt: A friend who's learning to program asks why the fraud checker saw a payment as captured but the email program, a moment later, didn't, "if both read the same database, and every read asks a majority of the copies". Explain it in plain words.
explain.answer: The database keeps three copies of each payment. When the capture was written, it reached one copy quickly and the other two a little later, and the write only counts as finished once two copies have it. The fraud checker asked all three copies, got its first two answers from the fast copy and a slow one, and took the newer value: captured. The email program started after that, asked again, and got its first two answers from the two slow copies, which still said authorized. A majority only promises that you see writes that have finished. This one was still on its way, and the fraud checker saw it early. To rule this out, a read that sees a newer value has to copy it to a second copy before answering, so every read takes two round trips instead of one. For decisions, it's simpler to read from one leader, so there's only one copy to ask.

deeper.html:
Answers that never came. Wing and Gong's search treats a timed-out operation as the hard case. If a client sent a write and never heard back, the write may or may not have happened, at any moment after it was sent. Checkers give such an operation an end time of infinity, and let the search either place it anywhere after its start or leave it out. That's why Jepsen's histories mark each operation :ok, :fail or :info (unknown), and why your own retry code should record "unknown" outcomes instead of guessing.

Seeing a failed check. Porcupine's README explains its speed-ups and shows the picture it draws for a failed check: the longest partial linearization, with the operations it couldn't place. MIT's 6.5840 course on distributed systems uses it to grade students' Raft key-value stores.

Lincheck on your own classes. Lincheck runs @Operation methods from several threads and compares the results with every one-at-a-time run. Its model-checking mode switches between threads itself, so a failure comes with an exact order of steps you can replay in IntelliJ. Try it on a class you wrote with @Volatile fields and a check-then-act: it usually finds the race in seconds.

Further reading. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 10, covers linearizability, the quorum race and the cost of linearizable systems.
